title: The Greek and Latin alphabet concordance from Pontigny
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: Cleveland records a leaf from a copy of Gratian’s Decretum. Four arches on this side hold matching Greek and Latin letter forms. The leaf is dated around 1160–1165.
limit: A match between letter forms is not a translation of the legal text. The museum says this leaf could have belonged to the copy Thomas Becket consulted.
alt: Four decorated arches hold aligned columns of letters.
basis: This leaf uses columns to help a reader find matching signs.
check: Bring the index back to the same mark on both lines.
answer: Ansel finds the matched sign. He asks Mera to read the instruction itself before he moves any crate.
returnFocus: which two signs share one line
use: Align the paired sign stops on Venn’s guide.
returnResult: A reader can recover the same sign from either entry. Venn leaves the meaning of the instruction in its own slot.
outside: Bring the bundle marked by the west sign.
inside: The west sign has a match on the other guide. Both marks point to one bundle on the west rail.

title: Mughal School Exercise Alphabet
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
languages: Alphabet practice in a Mughal manuscript
fact: Cleveland records these pages as a School Exercise Alphabet from Mughal India in the 1700s.
limit: The group of practice pages cannot show how every pupil learned, which words they first read, or who wrote them.
alt: Several examples of handwritten letter shapes are arranged on manuscript pages.
basis: A short set of examples can teach a form before it carries a finished message.
check: Move the sample shapes out of the delivery line.
answer: Ansel matches the letter shapes from the sample pocket and reads the finished tag on a separate line.
returnFocus: where an example stops and a delivery begins
use: Give the letter sample its own raised edge.
returnResult: The two pockets now tell a learner which shapes are for practice and which narrow strip they can carry.
outside: Carry the red peg after lunch.
inside: The repeated lines under the card are for practice. The single red peg on the top line is the one the south runner needs.

title: Leaf from the Farhang-i Jahangiri Persian dictionary
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The museum names Mir Jamal al-Din Husayn Inju as compiler of the Persian dictionary. It shows this illuminated folio from the Mughal court and reports that the dictionary supplied definitions and examples from Persian poets.
limit: One folio preserves a set of entries. It cannot settle what every Persian reader in court or elsewhere meant by a given word.
alt: An illuminated manuscript leaf with ruled columns, heading, and compact Persian entries.
basis: A cited line can show how a word worked in a sentence.
check: Pin the example next to the shorter definition.
answer: Ansel keeps the short sense for a loading note and leaves the longer example by the reader’s lamp.
returnFocus: how the example supports one meaning
use: Open the example flap beside the short definition.
returnResult: Venn places the familiar word beside a line a visitor can check. A reader can ask for the use outside that line.
outside: Bring the spare handle, not the fitted one.
inside: The word spare can mean an unused part or a part someone can lend. Ask for the unused handle from the lower drawer.

title: Hemachandra’s Great Poem about Twos, folio 2
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
fact: Cleveland dates this folio to 1428. It names Hemachandra as author of the work, which used examples of a patron’s deeds to illustrate grammar, and Abhayatilaka as commentator.
limit: The catalogue distinguishes the earlier composition and the later folio. Literary praise serves an example and does not verify every deed independently.
alt: A red-ground manuscript leaf with illustrated figures and several inscribed lines.
basis: A story can make a grammar pattern easier to see.
check: Try the pattern with another worker’s name in the same slot.
answer: Ansel leaves the instruction with the new name. The example stays in its pocket as an example.
returnFocus: which place in the wording tells a reader who acts
use: Set the example above the sender’s blank name slot.
returnResult: Venn tries the line with a second named carrier. Readers can see what remains the same when a person changes.
outside: Tell Neris to bring the third tray.
inside: Our practice line names Orla at first. Replace her name with Neris. The person named has the tray job in this line.

title: Sri Lankan palm-leaf manuscript
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The museum describes a palm-leaf manuscript from Sri Lanka around 1700. Its writing is incised in the surface and darkened. The support and the letter forms are separate features of this record.
limit: The record describes the object and its support. The photograph alone does not identify what all its lines say or which readings were public.
alt: Long, narrow palm leaves with repeated horizontal lines and aligned holes.
basis: A writing support can decide which side of a narrow line the reader opens first.
check: Give the first line a place where the edge can be found.
answer: Ansel lines up the marked end before reading. The returning note keeps that starting point.
returnFocus: where a narrow line begins
use: Seat the long note against a marked end stop.
returnResult: Venn can turn the practice card back after it slips. Its same starting end reaches the next reader.
outside: Start at the notched end of the long slip.
inside: Begin where the near stop meets the edge. The visible line points to a bundle behind the second peg.

title: Muhammad Shah Qajar’s calligraphy practice leaf
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met dates the page to Shawwal 1260 AH, October 1844. It names Muhammad Shah Qajar as the calligrapher. He used verses from the Shahnama in a nasta’liq exercise. A separate inscription dedicates the leaf to Khadija Khanum.
limit: The repetitions belong to calligraphy practice. The separate dedication identifies an addressee for this leaf.
alt: An album leaf with repeated, slanting Persian script and a decorative surround.
basis: A form copied several times and the dedication can have different readers.
check: Fold the repeated practice forms away from the recipient’s line.
answer: Ansel finds the recipient without treating every repeated phrase as another request.
returnFocus: which line identifies the recipient
use: Put the dedication line at the entrance to the practice note.
returnResult: Venn’s next reader can find the addressee. The exercises stay available on their own leaf.
outside: Put the dedication on its own named line.
inside: The practice words repeat across the page. Keep the dedication up front so the runner knows who was meant to receive the leaf.

title: Govardhan illustration from a Persian Bhagavata Purana
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: Cleveland identifies this Deccan painting as an illustration connected with a Persian translation of the Bhagavata Purana. Its catalogue dates this physical painting to the 1700s and the translation context in the title to around 1625.
limit: The painting’s date and the translation context refer to different parts of the record. The display keeps its Hindu subject and devotional context distinct from the fictional delivery practice.
alt: A painting with a central figure carrying Mount Govardhan above a group of people.
basis: A painting can help a reader locate an episode while the translated words follow another route.
check: Send the visual locator with a separate path to the wording.
answer: Ansel uses the picture to find the entry. The message he can quote comes from a named copy at the staffed desk.
returnFocus: where a picture locates an episode and where its wording lives
use: Clip the painted locator beside the translation’s dated catalogue line.
returnResult: A reader can find the scene quickly. Venn’s older stand also keeps a way to recover the separate wording and date.
outside: Find the entry by its illustration.
inside: The picture locates the episode. The separate dated record leads to the translation named in the catalogue.

title: Redon’s 1896 La Maison hantée title plate
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The title plate credits Bulwer-Lytton’s text and René Philipon’s French translation. The museum also describes artist Odilon Redon’s collaboration with printer Auguste Clot on the lithographs.
limit: This is the title plate for the set. It does not disclose what every later reader thought of the English story, the French text or the prints.
alt: A lithographic title plate with text credits and a shadowed image.
basis: A title can name the people behind a text and a new way of reading it.
check: Open the translator’s line before forwarding the title.
answer: Ansel leaves separate credit for the wording and for the picture. His reply makes it clear which part he can reuse.
returnFocus: who supplied the words of the carried version
use: Place author, translator and print roles on separate tabs.
returnResult: A returning reader now finds the translated words without passing the printer off as their author.
outside: Send the French reading to the evening reader.
inside: The cover credits the earlier writer, the translator, the pictured reading and the printer separately. Send the words from the translator’s strip.

title: The letter pi on an 1084 Greek manuscript leaf
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: Cleveland records thirteen lines of Greek on this Psalter and New Testament leaf. The initial pi is formed by two figures. The museum describes similarities to manuscript work in Constantinople.
limit: The figure serves as an initial in this context. It does not supply how the full text would have sounded in every setting.
alt: A decorated Greek leaf where two figures form the large initial over smaller lines.
basis: A marked opening can identify where to start without retelling the line.
check: Send the start mark with the short reading direction.
answer: Ansel finds the first line from its start mark. He can ask separately what the words mean.
returnFocus: which route mark is a start marker
use: Fit the opening marker in the entrance pocket.
returnResult: The next runner’s reply identifies the first line instead of taking the picture for an instruction.
outside: Open to the page with the joined beginning sign.
inside: The figure gives the start mark. Read the small line below it to find the time a reader should meet the carrier.

title: Speech of Rishabhadatta, Kalpa-sutra folio 5
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
languages: Text and transliteration from a Jain manuscript
fact: Cleveland records both sides of this leaf, with an illustration of celestial dancers on the recto and the speech in writing. It supplies a transcription alongside its object description.
limit: The leaf belongs to a Jain scripture. Its pictured and transcribed parts are documented here as distinct ways to encounter the leaf. Neither is reenacted.
alt: An illustrated manuscript leaf with dancers and separate areas of writing.
basis: The location of a pictured opening and the reading of a written line are separate findings.
check: Turn the practice leaf before deciding which line the reply refers to.
answer: Ansel can point to a single written line instead of replying to whichever side is on top.
returnFocus: which face a reader refers to
use: Add side marks to Venn’s two practice flaps.
returnResult: A visitor can turn the note and describe the exact face. The older source line remains on its own pocket.
outside: Turn the practice leaf for the written reply.
inside: The facing illustration helps a visitor find the sheet. The reply goes with the line on the numbered side, not whichever face lies upwards.

title: Persian Benefits of Animals leaf, ringdoves and quails
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The museum records a Persian Benefits of Animals manuscript leaf. The two faces concern different birds, ringdoves on one and quails on the other.
limit: The title identifies subjects on this leaf. It does not imply that claims in an earlier treatise are contemporary observations.
alt: A manuscript leaf showing illustrated birds and lines of Persian text.
basis: A surviving face can relate to a different subject than the one behind it.
check: Ask Ansel to name the face he opened before he says which bundle he needs.
answer: Ansel replies with the position of the requested card. The reverse stays available for a different delivery.
returnFocus: which subject belongs on each face
use: Fit a named subject tab to each face of the two-sided note.
returnResult: Venn leaves both entries together but a runner can choose the right face before copying a direction.
outside: Take the request on the pigeon side.
inside: The reverse has its own item label for a different delivery. Keep the requested face with the message until the desk checks the number.

title: Kangxi dish with a gift inscription and Xiang River picture
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The museum records a short Chinese inscription on this dish that presents an image of the Xiang River to another person. The picture and gift wording share the object.
limit: The gift wording does not identify a known separate delivery or prove which individual took the dish.
alt: A painted dish with a small water landscape and a short inscription.
basis: A delivery named in a gift line can carry an image without sending the thing pictured.
check: Read back what the receiver is being offered.
answer: Ansel takes the picture copy and leaves the object represented by it on the record shelf.
returnFocus: what the person actually receives
use: Seat the gift wording below the pictured reference.
returnResult: Venn’s reader takes the picture notice and leaves the object to its own catalogue. Both references point back to the account.
outside: Offer the picture of the route.
inside: The gift is a drawing of the crossing. The route itself remains open, and the signed chart stays at the desk.

title: Semi-cursive calligraphy with an opening mark
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The museum transcribes the opening mark and a paired line in semi-cursive Chinese script. Its catalogue distinguishes the script style and the language of its text.
limit: Connecting and simplifying strokes changes their appearance. This does not by itself make another language or change the stated time.
alt: A hanging scroll with several vertical lines of dark cursive forms.
basis: A new practical hand can make the same written clue look unfamiliar.
check: Match the practice line to the same starting phrase in the steadier hand.
answer: Ansel keeps a matching start mark and uses the nearest readable version of the same note.
returnFocus: how to link two hands to one instruction
use: Pin a matching start mark across the regular and flowing lines.
returnResult: The next reader translates the unfamiliar form into the same movement. Venn’s two slips still refer to one job.
outside: The flowing line and the regular line both call for the peg.
inside: Their opening looks different. Put one locator in both forms so a reader can recover the same instruction.

title: Scroll from Xuanzang’s translation of the Abhidharmakosha-Bhashya
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
languages: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit work
fact: Cleveland identifies this Japanese scroll as part seventeen of Xuanzang’s thirty-part Chinese translation of a work associated with the Indian scholar Vasubandhu.
limit: The identities of the earlier author and translator do not alone establish who copied this surviving scroll. Its display does not reproduce the religious instructions.
alt: A narrow manuscript scroll with ordered lines of writing.
basis: A translated work can travel and be copied again with a section number still attached.
check: Tie the section number and translator’s role to the working line.
answer: Ansel can find the relevant section without assigning the new copy to the earlier writer.
returnFocus: which writer, translator and copy each register names
use: Set a stepped register for author, translation and surviving copy.
returnResult: Venn keeps an archive space for the translator and a different shelf for the surviving copy. A note can now travel between them.
outside: Bring the reader to section seventeen.
inside: The later copy, earlier work and translation each have an entry. A reader can find this section through the translation tab.

title: Seal of Venetian Doge Michele Steno
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: Cleveland describes a seal with an inscription naming Doge Michele Steno. It was attached to a charter issued in 1409. The museum records physical date and charter connection separately.
limit: The seal can support who issued a charter when paired with its records. It cannot give all the charter’s clauses on its own.
alt: A round patterned seal with figures, lettering around the rim and a central relief.
basis: An authority mark belongs to a role and a particular handover.
check: Clip the sender’s mark next to the named order it actually signs.
answer: Ansel can say whose order reached the rack. He leaves the recipient’s own witness line blank until its separate reply arrives.
returnFocus: which record the seal supports
use: Give the authority mark one matched slot beside the signed order.
returnResult: Venn’s reader can recover the authorised wording without expecting the stamp to speak for the practice test.
outside: Carry the order whose seal fits the upper slot.
inside: The seal names the person issuing it. The keeper’s answer will have its own line under the order.

title: Limestone plaque for Julia Donata with Latin and Greek inscriptions
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met describes a first-century Cypriot funerary plaque naming Julia Donata. It records a Latin description of her burial and a Greek farewell below. The two use their respective commemorative conventions.
limit: The two lines refer to one person and need not mirror every word. The plaque does not supply the rest of Julia Donata’s biography.
alt: A stone plaque with two physically separate lines of inscription.
basis: Corresponding lines can keep a name while giving a different form of address.
check: Show the shared name and read back what the greeting does on each line.
answer: Ansel checks who both lines name. He remembers that a welcome on his receiving side has a different job than a description.
returnFocus: which parts travel across both forms
use: Clip the common name across the paired forms and give each greeting its own strip.
returnResult: The two greetings can keep their different jobs. Venn’s reader still returns the note to the same person.
outside: Leave both greetings for the same named reader.
inside: One line tells the visitor where the copy rests, the other welcomes the next reader. Keep the named addressee across both forms.

title: Sehetepibre bilingual cylinder seal fragment
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
languages: Hieroglyphic Egyptian and a second name
fact: The Met describes a lapis lazuli cylinder seal fragment naming Sehetepibre in Egyptian hieroglyphs. It also reads the name Yakin-ilum on the opposite side.
limit: The catalogue connects the names to different people. Two marks on one piece do not make the two roles interchangeable.
alt: A small blue stone cylinder fragment with carefully incised marks.
basis: A place stamp and a person’s name need different places on a work card.
check: Preserve both sides and show which mark starts the reply.
answer: Ansel reads the name from the opposite face. He leaves the other mark attached as source rather than signing with it.
returnFocus: who belongs to each face
use: Attach the second name where the practice cylinder turns.
returnResult: Venn can keep both faces discoverable without assigning the second person’s work to the first.
outside: Read the name on the second face before returning the packet.
inside: Each side has its own named record. The reader signs below the face they consulted.

title: Urra=hubullu tablet 13, vocabulary of domestic animals
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met identifies this as an Urra=hubullu vocabulary tablet for domestic animals. It catalogues the physical tablet around the late first millennium BCE.
limit: The record is evidence of how one bilingual vocabulary was organised. It does not establish when every listed term was used in ordinary speech.
alt: A brown clay tablet with horizontal areas of impressed wedge-shaped writing.
basis: A vocabulary list can help find an exact word when a general heading gives too little.
check: Bring the particular animal entry beside the crate name.
answer: Ansel matches the exact entry and puts the broad heading back in the index.
returnFocus: what work a general heading can do
use: Move the exact animal tag inside its named index pocket.
returnResult: An older search now reaches a named entry instead of handing its carrier a whole shelf of possible terms.
outside: Bring the card for the small pack animal.
inside: Use the entry for this named animal. The broad pen heading is enough to find the shelf, and the recipient needs the card inside it.

title: Urra=hubullu tablet 23, vocabulary of food and drink
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met identifies this as the twenty-third tablet of a series, with food and drink terms first in Sumerian and then in Akkadian translation. Its partial form preserves three columns.
limit: The list suggests scholarly categories and terms. It does not record what one household had for a meal.
alt: A broken clay tablet with small wedge-shaped marks in vertical columns.
basis: A second language can be aligned with the first without changing which entry the reader is following.
check: Keep the two food words at the same notch before the runner carries the short line.
answer: Ansel lines up the entry and directs the carrier to the correct tagged box, leaving the translation’s broader context behind a tab.
returnFocus: which entries share a vocabulary row
use: Line up the food tag and its paired form against the same guide.
returnResult: A reader can follow either form to the right item. The practice list remains a separate reference from the live order.
outside: Follow the drink entry beside the red peg.
inside: The same row carries two words for the entry. Leave the row marker with the request, even if the runner reads one side first.

title: Later copy of Sin-sharra-ishkun’s letter to Nabopolassar
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
fact: The Met identifies this tablet as a second-century BCE copy of a letter originally composed late in the seventh century BCE. It explains the unusual address used for Nabopolassar in the surviving text.
limit: The copied letter is evidence of the sender’s wording as preserved. The recipient’s own lettered reply has not survived in this account.
alt: Brown, fitted fragments with lines of cuneiform on their exposed faces.
basis: A copied request has a date and a sender. It cannot supply the answer by itself.
check: Keep the reply clip clear until Ansel makes his own mark.
answer: Ansel sends a separate reply instead of signing under the copied request.
returnFocus: how the copy date differs from the reply’s date
use: Set distinct date hooks for the older request and its actual reply.
returnResult: Venn’s apprentice can file the copied wording with its own date. The remaining opening belongs to a separate answer.
outside: Send an acknowledgement for the copied letter.
inside: Clip the dated copy as a request. Leave the second space ready for the response that the actual recipient sends.

title: Amarna letter sent by Ashur-uballit
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met describes this as a letter by Ashur-uballit in an Assyrian dialect of Akkadian, sent with a messenger and gifts to the Egyptian court. The museum names Akhenaten as the probable recipient.
limit: The diplomatic letter gives the sender’s communication. It does not directly show how its proposed relationship was received.
alt: An inscribed clay letter densely marked with wedge-shaped writing.
basis: A messenger’s job can be explicit even when the reply is not known.
check: Give the messenger a copy that keeps the recipient distinct from their own name.
answer: Ansel’s return names the recipient and leaves a line for the next messenger to sign separately.
returnFocus: which name belongs to the messenger
use: Fit the messenger’s slip in its own crossbar pocket.
returnResult: The runner can take a handover receipt without overwriting which reader the letter was for.
outside: Bring the packet to the named keeper.
inside: The runner carries the gift and request. The person at the far desk is the addressee and supplies the answer.

title: Amarna letter sent by Abi-milku of Tyre
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met describes this Akkadian letter from Abi-milku, ruler of Tyre, to the Egyptian king. Its catalogue explains that the letter conveys an expectation of protection along with loyalty.
limit: That expectation belongs to the sender’s message. This record alone does not verify that the requested protection followed.
alt: A clay letter with fitted areas of cuneiform and uneven edges.
basis: A statement of loyalty and a requested action should remain separately answerable.
check: Point to the request beside the greeting before asking for a reply.
answer: Ansel acknowledges the greeting and sends the specific request to the desk that can act on it.
returnFocus: which part of the note asks for action
use: Make a separate destination tab for the request below its greeting.
returnResult: The return record shows that the message reached its reader. It leaves the requested action open until a separate receipt arrives.
outside: Acknowledge the greeting and take the request below it.
inside: Keep the commitment on the first strip. Send the requested help to the person who can say whether it is possible.

title: Bilingual Coptic-Arabic Psalm folio
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met identifies this Egyptian folio as Psalm 15. It says the wide left column is Coptic and the narrower right column is the Arabic translation. The historical object is displayed with its own devotional context.
limit: Column width does not make one language the only reader’s entry. The fictional dispatch work copies a layout idea and does not rehearse the psalm.
alt: A leaf with a wide left writing column and a narrow right one.
basis: A wide source column and its narrow translation can point to one line.
check: Put a locator at the line shared by the two practice columns.
answer: Ansel can check the source line with the reader who starts from the short column.
returnFocus: how unequal columns can share a line
use: Place one line keeper across the wide and narrow columns.
returnResult: A visitor keeps the original locator even if they enter by the short column. The page stays a shared reference.
outside: Keep the left and right lines at the same number.
inside: One column is broader. Hold the pointer at the same place for the reader who begins on the narrow side.

title: Gennadius’s letter to Peter on a potsherd
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met records a letter from Gennadius to Peter on a potsherd and publishes a translation in which Gennadius asks about eggs and says he sent money with a servant.
limit: The letter gives a particular request and names its readers. It does not show that eggs were obtained or the journey completed.
alt: A small fragment of pottery with dark lines of handwriting.
basis: The person asked to act and the person carrying something may be different.
check: Match the request to its reader and the sending slip to the carrier.
answer: Ansel records who should act. A separate delivery clip records who carried the bundle.
returnFocus: where a carrier’s entry sits beside the addressee
use: Separate the addressee tabs from the carrier peg.
returnResult: Venn keeps the bundle with the carrier slip and sends the actual request to the named receiver.
outside: Ask Peter about the eggs. Match the money to the carrier slip.
inside: The sender’s request goes to Peter. The person who brings the bundle needs a different signed line.

title: Middle Persian fragment of King Narseh’s bilingual inscription
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
languages: Middle Persian from a bilingual inscription
fact: The Met records this stone from Paikuli in present-day Iraq as a fragment in Middle Persian script from a bilingual inscription of King Narseh. It dates the object to 293–302 CE.
limit: The stone is one surviving part of the inscription. It does not display the intact wording of both versions.
alt: A low stone fragment shows worn rows of script along an irregular edge.
basis: A fragment can have a precise place in a wider record and still leave a line open.
check: Add a clear place mark for the part that survived.
answer: Ansel files one readable piece and leaves an open mark for its undocumented match.
returnFocus: where a fragment’s reading ends
use: Add the end stop for the surviving words and leave the missing pocket open.
returnResult: The next reader only repeats the segment supported by the record. The second empty pocket can take a separate source later.
outside: Send only the surviving words on the marked card.
inside: The other half of the wrapper is unknown. Leave a pocket for a second record if somebody brings one.

title: Musō Soseki’s letter to Suwa Daishin
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
languages: Formal written Chinese used in Japan
fact: The Met records that Musō Soseki used formal Chinese for a letter to Suwa Daishin, an Ashikaga shogunate official, and discusses its later mounting. The letter requests a reply about a previous land matter.
limit: The form and recipient help explain the register. They do not supply the otherwise unspecified exact year or the official’s answer.
alt: A written letter with vertical brush lines mounted within decorative cloth.
basis: An administrative reply can have more than one useful form of address.
check: Put the formal addressee on the reading line before naming the earlier matter.
answer: Ansel can tell the runner whom to ask. The mounting strip shows an earlier paperwork reference instead of inventing an answer.
returnFocus: what the formal address is for
use: Rest the formal address at the official reply peg.
returnResult: An earlier notice now gives a visitor the recipient’s role and a path back to the earlier note.
outside: Put the reply with the official, not the person who mounted the slip.
inside: The old note asks the responsible officer to answer a separate request. The decorative backing has its own entry.

title: Transcription of Zekkai Chūshin’s letter to Shippei Shikai
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
languages: Written letter from a Japanese Zen community
fact: The Met describes this as a transcription by an unidentified scribe of words composed by Zekkai Chūshin. It distinguishes the surviving brushwork from Zekkai’s known hand. The letter congratulates Shippei Shikai.
limit: The thanks and congratulations belong to the earlier author’s content. The physical strokes on this copy cannot be credited to him solely because it preserves the wording.
alt: A paper handscroll with upright rows of brush writing.
basis: A surviving transcript can preserve a voice and a separate person’s working hand.
check: Point the sender tab to the author and the copy tab to the surviving hand.
answer: Ansel signs for the copy. He leaves the greeting credited to the person who composed it.
returnFocus: whose hand made the copy
use: Put the copied strokes under a separate attribution flap.
returnResult: Venn’s reader can follow the live instruction and still tell whose wording and whose copied page they are holding.
outside: Keep the greeting under the sender’s name and the copy under its own credit.
inside: The scribe’s hand made the surviving page. The greeting still belongs to the person whose letter was transcribed.

title: Wen Zhengming’s letter to Wu Yu
dateKind: Dated surviving museum object or leaf. The date belongs to this catalogue record.
fact: The Met identifies this letter by Wen Zhengming to his father-in-law Wu Yu. It describes the deferential tone and stationery decorated with plum blossom motifs.
limit: The written voice addresses a particular person. The tone does not establish how Wen wrote or spoke with every audience.
alt: A narrow letter with fine handwriting against patterned stationery.
basis: A reader can keep a courteous register and still find the practical request.
check: Leave a separate reply tab for the line the recipient can act on.
answer: Ansel keeps the courteous opening on the card and sends a usable answer for the task below it.
returnFocus: how a courteous line sits with a practical reply
use: Fit the courteous opening above the short returning instruction.
returnResult: A visitor can recover the tone without missing the route they came to find.
outside: Keep the salutation and bring me the bottom line.
inside: The first wording is courteous to an older relative. The lower line lets this particular reader answer the practical request.

title: Bound Hadith manuscript with Jami’s Persian translations
date: Manuscript dated 935 AH/1528 CE; binding ca. 1575–1600
dateKind: The manuscript has a date from its copying inscription. The Met gives a later approximate date for its binding.
fact: The Met credits Shah Mahmud Nishapuri with the copying of this manuscript in Tabriz, dated 1528, and the Persian translation to poet Jami. It separately dates the surviving binding, around 1575–1600.
limit: The distinct dates and names describe copying, translating and binding. The fictional practice uses separate role tabs instead of reenacting the traditions.
alt: An illuminated bound manuscript with diagonal fields between ruled lines.
basis: A reader can keep original wording and translated wording with distinct credits.
check: Frame the translated working line and keep the original attribution separate.
answer: Ansel uses the fold prepared for his reading and leaves both credits visible to the keeper.
returnFocus: how to distinguish copied part and translated part
use: Lay a narrow role line below each differently angled practice strip.
returnResult: Venn’s stand preserves the earlier wording’s source and the change made to reach the second reader.
outside: Give the reader the translated working line.
inside: Leave the original’s locator, the translator’s role and the later copying credit together in separate spaces.

title: Hokusai’s Quick Pictorial Dictionary
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The Met catalogues the two-volume Quick Pictorial Dictionary, dated 1819. It credits Katsushika Hokusai and publisher Kakumaruya Jinsuke.
limit: The pictorial approach is part of this work. A picture alone does not give every possible reading of a Japanese term.
alt: A printed Japanese book shows small picture examples arranged across the page.
basis: A small picture can help a reader find a word without acting as a full direction.
check: Use the picture as a locator and match the return to the named item.
answer: Ansel finds the expected line at the matching picture. He reads the actual place from the words on the letter.
returnFocus: how a learner moves from picture to word
use: Join the quick picture locator to the named item with a short edge clip.
returnResult: A visitor can search by shape or by the name. Venn leaves the actual instruction under its separate heading.
outside: Find the little handle picture. Read the name beside it.
inside: The picture guides the search. The written name takes the carrier to the specific drawer that holds the item.

title: On the Seventeenth Day, a later rubbing of Wang Xizhi’s letters
date: 13th-century rubbing of a series of 4th-century texts
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
fact: The Met discusses this 13th-century rubbing of a selection of earlier correspondence by Wang Xizhi. The surviving rubbing comes through earlier copies and preserves an imperial order mark.
limit: The rubbing is a distinct physical object and source. Its date and the order mark cannot date the original letters to the thirteenth century.
alt: A dark-backed album of rubbings with bright gaps forming lines of characters.
basis: Official backing of a later copy cannot turn it into the author’s first hand.
check: Keep one date for the surviving copy and one place for the earlier letter.
answer: Ansel signs receipt of the rubbing-based example. The original author and the marking of official copying remain distinct.
returnFocus: the stages a copied letter passed through
use: Place the later reproduction number next to the date of copying.
returnResult: A reader can follow the transmission history and leave the earlier paper’s exact fate in an open record.
outside: File the rubbing as a copy, with the old letter name beside it.
inside: The copy carries a later official mark. Keep that mark and the earlier author on distinct lines.

title: Alhambra survey with translated Arabic inscriptions, volume one
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The Met’s volume one records architectural drawings from the 1830s in an English-language publication issued 1842–1845. The title credits Jules Goury, Owen Jones and work on the inscriptions and history to Pascual de Gayangos.
limit: The book joins a survey and a translation. Its publisher’s dates do not establish the dates of all the buildings or inscriptions it records.
alt: A printed architectural volume with an engraved illustrated page and carefully ruled details.
basis: A plan locator and a translated line can have different creators and dates.
check: Match the mark on the drawing to the line that has its own credit.
answer: Ansel finds where to look on the practice map. He reads the wording from its labelled line rather than from the outline.
returnFocus: who supplied an inscription reading and who drew its support
use: Place a locator on the drawing that opens its own credited line.
returnResult: The older guide now reaches the appropriate view and leaves the inscription reader, surveyor and dates in separate roles.
outside: Use the drawn arch to find the inscription row.
inside: The drawing shows where the record belongs. Its reader and draughtsman have separate credits and dates.

title: Spanish City of God manuscript
dateKind: The museum dates this physical copy or leaf. The composition or work it transmits has a separate history.
fact: The Met records this as one of three volumes of a Spanish translation of Augustine’s Latin City of God. Its catalogue describes large initials, marginal notes and short explanations after sections.
limit: The surviving volume is a later translation with reader aids. A margin does not automatically have the same speaker or authority as the central text.
alt: An illuminated Spanish manuscript page with a large initial and tight written columns.
basis: An editor’s explanation may help a new reader without replacing the line it explains.
check: Put the explanation beside the message rather than over its words.
answer: Ansel carries the short explanation and keeps a path to the wording on the main fold.
returnFocus: where a translated statement gives way to a reader’s explanation
use: Make the commentary strip lift without hiding the earlier line.
returnResult: A reader can use the shorter help and open the main wording when the explanation alone leaves a question.
outside: Read the explanatory strip beside the main fold.
inside: The smaller note helps the visitor. Open the central wording when someone needs to check which idea the note explains.

title: Isenberg’s Amharic grammar, Wellcome copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: Wellcome holds Charles William Isenberg’s printed Grammar of the Amharic Language, published in London in 1842. The shelfmark and digital record identify this copy.
limit: A grammar prepared in the nineteenth century has its own authorship and purpose. This copy does not stand for all varieties of Amharic or for present-day usage.
alt: A photographed page from a small nineteenth-century printed grammar.
basis: A reading guide gives someone a starting form without predicting every later use.
check: Align the sample and the address before taking the short instruction.
answer: Ansel checks the printed starting form and sends the named recipient’s request with a separate clarifying note.
returnFocus: which mark belongs to the grammar guide
use: Set one raised origin tab at the left of the guide line.
returnResult: Venn’s next learner finds a way to begin the reading and keeps the practice guide apart from the delivery note.
outside: Try the marked starting form before calling the runner.
inside: A practice pattern gives the learner a way in. Keep the named addressee on a different line when the live request goes out.

title: Titus Lewis’s Welsh-English dictionary, second edition
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: Wellcome records this as a second edition of Titus Lewis’s Welsh-English dictionary, printed in Carmarthen in 1815. Its title names both languages.
limit: This specifically dated second edition is one reader’s tool. It is not proof that a listed equivalence works in every context.
alt: A digitised early nineteenth-century dictionary page with small close-set type.
basis: A reader can use an equivalent to get started and come back for the longer sense.
check: Seat the short equivalent beside the phrase it is meant to carry.
answer: Ansel can give a quick answer while a second reader checks the wording from the longer entry.
returnFocus: where the short phrase keeps its applicable use
use: Insert the example tab between the word and delivery instruction.
returnResult: Venn leaves the smaller equivalent beside an actual use. He gives the larger sense a different fold.
outside: Use the short equivalent where the waiting reader can see it.
inside: The full entry supplies a longer sense. Keep the line that tells the learner which meaning helps in this situation.

title: Peter Breton’s five-language vocabulary, Wellcome copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
languages: English, Arabic, Persian, Hindi and Sanskrit
fact: Wellcome identifies this 1825 vocabulary printed in Calcutta for members of a medical department. It lists English, Arabic, Persian, Hindi and Sanskrit in the title and identifies Peter Breton as compiler.
limit: The institutional glossary is historical. The game uses no medical procedures or claims from it. One column’s words do not give the full scope of another.
alt: A digitised page of a printed multi-language vocabulary showing lines in separate scripts.
basis: Several language columns need one clear locator when a line moves between them.
check: Keep the row number with the wording sent to the other desk.
answer: Ansel can map the short line back to the intended row before asking a reader to act.
returnFocus: how a row can survive switching column
use: Set one movable ruler across all the practice columns.
returnResult: Venn can hand a reader their starting column and preserve a pointer to where the other column shares a row.
outside: Keep the row when you move to the reader’s other column.
inside: The method is borrowed from the printed arrangement. Our practice rows name stock at the dispatch desk and have no medical instructions.

title: Arenas’s 1611 Spanish–Nahuatl manual, Newberry Ayer copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The Newberry holds Pedro de Arenas’s 1611 vocabulary manual in Spanish and Nahuatl, identified by its Ayer shelfmark. Its title presents common questions and replies as a practical aid in colonial-era communication.
limit: The compiler’s book records a particular encounter and purpose. Its terms should not be treated as the words of all Nahuatl speakers or as instructions for present-day life.
alt: A title or early printed page from an individually identified old volume.
basis: A practice phrase can invite an answer rather than assume what another person will say.
check: Clip space for the recipient’s reply under the short asking line.
answer: Ansel separates the supplied example answer from the response given by the person he actually met.
returnFocus: where a question ends and an answer can begin
use: Add the spare reply fold below the old phrase line.
returnResult: Venn’s copy leaves room for a reader’s actual answer. It no longer routes the example reply as though it had been received.
outside: Carry a question with room for an answer.
inside: The example reply helps a learner practise. Leave a blank fold so the actual reader can tell the runner what to bring.

title: 1915 grammar of dialect changes in Kiswahili, Toronto copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The Toronto deposit records a 1915 Kiswahili grammar printed by Cambridge University Press and lists C. H. Stigand and W. E. Taylor. The title also records a recension and poetic translation of Inkishafi.
limit: The English rendering and this author’s description of dialects are distinct tasks. They do not make one printed form a universal standard.
alt: A scanned page from the 1915 grammar held at the University of Toronto.
basis: Useful words and poetic rendering can serve different rooms.
check: Send the standing instruction separately from the fuller literary line.
answer: Ansel can perform the narrow instruction and still send a reader to the fuller wording for what it adds.
returnFocus: which parts of an explanation serve different readers
use: Fit a shallow work pocket beside the longer poetic note.
returnResult: A runner takes the work line and the reading group can still find the text in its own place.
outside: Use the plain work line on the trip.
inside: The fuller literary reading belongs to the same note and can stay at the lamp where a reader has time for it.

title: 1910 Swahili grammar and vocabulary, UC Libraries copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The University of California Libraries deposit identifies this 1910 grammar and vocabulary. Its title credits Mrs. F. Burt, and the archive records A. E. Burt in the creator field.
limit: Its lesson and vocabulary structure support one historical learning method. The catalogue does not identify every contributor or show how speakers use each term today.
alt: A digitised early-twentieth-century grammar page.
basis: A learner can use one sample sentence and one name guide for different jobs.
check: Put the sentence on the visible route and the reference words under its edge.
answer: Ansel uses the sample to read a direction out and leaves its individual word entries ready for further check.
returnFocus: where a short useful pattern lives next to a word list
use: Give the sentence frame a separate notch from the glossary.
returnResult: A learner can pull the frame during a delivery and recover the individual words at the fixed station.
outside: Take the useful sentence and keep the word list on the shelf.
inside: The beginner can read the sentence in context. The glossary stays as a place to check further examples.

title: Samuel Ajayi Crowther’s Yoruba grammar, Bavarian State Library copy
dateKind: Print or publication date of the catalogued copy or edition.
fact: The Bavarian State Library identifies its 1852 London copy of A grammar of the Yoruba language, by Samuel Ajayi Crowther, with its shelfmark and published title. The catalogue lists Yoruba and English.
limit: The book records Crowther’s analysis as a particular author. This display uses a game schematic and does not reproduce the library’s restricted image.
alt: Original game illustration of a small printed volume and an opening note.
basis: Keep a language learner’s guide with the name of the person who authored it.
check: Give the visitor a labelled path to the work’s named author before passing the guide along.
answer: Ansel’s reply identifies whose guide reached him and what the new reader found useful.
returnFocus: who shaped the guide that a learner receives
use: Add the author’s name to the label beside the learner’s starting line.
returnResult: Venn’s apprentice can find the exact named work before retelling what it can help a learner see.
outside: Give the learner a starting direction with a named author.
inside: The short reading aid points to Crowther’s exact guide. An older note without his name needs its own credit to be checkable.
